author: Claude Fable 5.1
_readme: One record per release, appended the day before it. `made` must precede `release_at` (tools/keycheck.py refuses otherwise). Each item names the bundle series and transform it is a call on; the page scores it against the figure as first printed. Never edit a record after its release. See CLAUDE.md, Forecasts.

items.label: Final demand
items.note: year over year, n.s.a., as the release prints it
items._added: 2026-09-09, later the same day, once the unadjusted series was catalogued; the s.a. call above is left as made

reasons: Energy turns from drag to push. The PPI is priced on the Tuesday of the week containing the 13th, so August against July is 11 August against 14 July: retail gasoline +3.9%, diesel +9.6%, WTI +4.1%, Brent +11.6%, Henry Hub flat. Over 2015–2026 the PPI gasoline index has moved 1.06× the retail move at those dates and final demand energy 0.35× PPI gasoline, so energy is put at about +2.5% s.a. after −6.5% in June and −3.1% in July. At its drifted weight of 5.7% that is roughly +0.14 points of the headline, and diesel’s outsized move is the upside risk to it.

Services less trade, transport and warehousing (about 44% of final demand) rose 0.6% in July on portfolio management +6.5%. The S&P 500 gained 2.7% in August, so that line stays positive but smaller, and the ISM services prices index at 72.6 was its highest since August 2022. Assumed +0.3%, worth +0.13 points.

Transport and warehousing fell 1.8% in July and 0.5% in June with fuel; with diesel and jet fuel up it is put at +1.0%, about +0.05 points. Core goods slowed to +0.13% in July from +0.7% and +0.8% in April and May as the Section 122 tariff pass-through peaked; the Section 301 duties that replaced them on 24 July are at similar rates and the ISM manufacturing prices index held at 71.1, so +0.3%, about +0.06 points.

Trade services are the swing factor and cannot be forecast. Margins run 19.8% of final demand, move with a monthly standard deviation of 0.88 points and an autocorrelation of −0.12, and they compressed when energy spiked (May −3.1%) and rebuilt when it fell (June +1.4%). A small +0.1% is assumed, worth +0.02 points; that one line puts about ±0.17 points on the headline by itself.
Foods fell 0.9% in July and are assumed to add back +0.2% (+0.01 points); construction jumped 2.2% in July on lumber and is assumed +0.2% (+0.01 points).

Adding up: about +0.41 points, so +0.4% for final demand. Without foods and energy the same parts sum to +0.27 points over 89% of the basket, +0.3%. Without trade services as well, +0.25 points over 69.7% is +0.35%, which rounds either way; it is called +0.3% on the services reversion rather than +0.4%, and this is the least certain of the four.

Year over year: August 2025 fell 0.18% s.a. (−0.29% n.s.a.) and drops out of the window, so the twelve-month rate rises by more than the month adds, from 4.7% to about 5.3% on the seasonally adjusted series this page draws; on the unadjusted basis the release prints, +0.4% for the month gives 5.4% and +0.3% gives 5.3%. Trader-implied odds were 73% on 5.1% or higher.

What would make this wrong: July’s 0.0% is itself revisable (PPI has revised 120 of the 139 months since 2015, median 0.13 index points); the headline’s monthly standard deviation over the last three years is 0.32 points, so ±0.3 is one sigma, and nearly all of it is trade margins and energy.
